headline: KSE-100 extends its rally to 181,777 as Wall Street retreats from records and oil jumps 4.9% on Iran's Hormuz conditions
mood: Cautiously constructive · oil's Hormuz conditions the swing factor

five_things.html: The KSE-100 gained 0.98% (+1,761.66 pts) to close at 181,776.59 on Thursday, a fourth straight advance, as broad-based buying continued across banks, oil & gas exploration, cement, fertiliser and power stocks; volume held firm at 345.78m shares (Rs40.31bn) with advancers outpacing decliners 75-to-25 among index constituents (Mettis Global, Trading Economics).

The Dow shed 464 points (−0.85%) to 53,885, while the S&P 500 slipped 0.18% to 7,709.96 and the Nasdaq eased 0.06% to 26,348.35, pulling back from this week's record highs as rising Treasury yields and a jump in oil prices weighed on sentiment (TheStreet, Washington Post).

Brent jumped 4.9% to $83.34 and WTI rose 3.37% to $77.75 after Iran's Foreign Ministry said any Strait of Hormuz reopening remains contingent on the US lifting its naval blockade, unwinding much of the week's de-escalation rally even as Tehran and Muscat agreed in principle on shipping-route coordinates (Bloomberg, Trading Economics).

Gold climbed to a seven-week high near $4,271 (+2.38%), its fourth straight advance, as softer US ADP jobs data lifted Fed rate-cut odds even as oil rebounded; silver added 0.6% to $61.83 (Fortune, Yahoo Finance).

Saudi's Public Investment Fund board approved its 2026-2030 strategy, pivoting from rapid project launches toward localisation, Saudisation and long-term industrial capability across six ecosystems, as July PMI held at 53.1 in Saudi Arabia and climbed to a four-month high of 52.7 in the UAE (PIF.gov.sa, Arab News).

matrix.local_html: Thursday's session saw the KSE-100 add 0.98% to close at 181,776.59, gaining 1,761.66 points as the rally that reclaimed 180,000 a day earlier extended into a fourth session. Breadth stayed constructive — 75 of 100 index constituents advanced against 25 decliners (282 gainers across the broader 494-company market) — on turnover of 345.78 million shares (Rs40.31bn), with commercial banks (+500.49 index points), oil & gas exploration (+264.49), cement (+251.19), fertiliser (+224.08) and power generation (+124.47) leading the advance; UBL, MARI, FFC, LUCK and BAHL were the biggest index contributors, while NPL, GADT, MLCF, PAEL and NML topped the gainers' board (Mettis Global). On the macro front, headline CPI eased to 9.2% YoY in July from 11.1% in June, giving the SBP room to hold its policy rate at 11.5% for a second straight meeting on 27 July. Six-month KIBOR is tracking near 11.70–11.90% (EST.), broadly in line with the policy rate. The IMF's Executive Board cleared the third EFF/second RSF review on 8 May, unlocking roughly $1.1bn (EFF) and $220m (RSF), with reform milestones including a new tax-audit manual due by end-August.
matrix.gcc_html: OPEC+'s seven-member subgroup agreed on 2 August to add a further 188,000 bpd from September, extending the gradual unwind of the April 2023 voluntary cuts even as the oil market stays jittery on Hormuz headlines. Gulf non-oil momentum held up in July: Saudi Arabia's non-oil PMI eased only slightly to 53.1 (53.3 in June) on firmer domestic demand, while the UAE's climbed to a four-month high of 52.7 from 50.8, with new business at a five-month high and employment growth returning. Saudi's Public Investment Fund board approved its 2026-2030 strategy, chaired by Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, pivoting from rapid capital deployment toward localisation, Saudisation and long-term industrial capability across six ecosystems including travel & tourism, urban development and NEOM. Oil itself reversed higher on the region's diplomacy: Brent jumped 4.9% to $83.34 and WTI rose 3.37% to $77.75 after Iran said a Hormuz reopening remains contingent on Washington lifting its naval blockade, unwinding much of this week's de-escalation rally.
matrix.global_html: Wall Street pulled back from this week's record highs: the Dow shed 464 points (−0.85%) to 53,885, the S&P 500 slipped 0.18% to 7,709.96 and the Nasdaq eased 0.06% to 26,348.35, as rising Treasury yields (10Y 4.61%, 2Y ~4.18%) and a jump in oil prices weighed on risk appetite even as softer US ADP jobs data kept September rate-cut hopes alive. Gold climbed to a seven-week high near $4,271 (+2.38%) and silver added 0.6% to $61.83 on the same haven bid. Washington's trade agenda keeps moving: a 50% Section 338 tariff on roughly $20bn of Canadian dairy, alcohol and motor-vehicle exports takes effect 19 August — now 12 days out — while Pakistan's own reciprocal tariff with the US remains a comparatively favourable 19%.

legislative.policy_html: Finance Act 2026's 5% withholding tax (10% for non-filers) on digital creators' social media earnings remains in force, with banks deducting it at source since 30 July; the IMF-linked reform calendar also has a new tax-audit manual and policy due by end-August.
legislative.impact_html: Wins: FBR compliance-tech vendors and formal-sector filers. Loses: non-filer creators facing the 10% deduction; compliance overhead builds ahead of the August audit-manual deadline.

legislative.policy_html: Saudi's PIF board approved its 2026-2030 strategy, pivoting from rapid capital deployment toward localisation and Saudisation, while OPEC+ added a further 188,000 bpd from September and Washington's Section 301 forced-labor duties (10–12.5% on roughly 60 economies including Saudi Arabia and the UAE) remain in force.
legislative.impact_html: Wins: domestic Saudi suppliers and localisation-ready contractors under the new PIF strategy. Loses: foreign contractors facing tighter localisation rules; Gulf exporters still absorbing forced-labor tariff exposure.

legislative.policy_html: The 50% US Section 338 tariff on Canadian dairy, alcohol and motor vehicles takes effect 19 August — now 12 days out, covering roughly $20bn of imports — barring a last-minute deal, while Pakistan's negotiated 19% reciprocal tariff with Washington remains in force.
legislative.impact_html: Wins: Pakistani textile and apparel exporters retaining a relative tariff advantage over higher-taxed peers. Loses: Canadian dairy, alcohol and auto exporters, and US importers/retailers facing the 19 August step-up.

levels.support_note: Wednesday's close, now first support; deeper support at 178,500 (Tuesday's intraday low)
levels.resistance_note: psychological round-number level; then the 2026 high of 189,167 set 23 January

desk_stance_html: Desk view: Thursday's 0.98% gain extended the KSE-100's rally to a fourth straight session on breadth-confirmed buying (75 advancers vs 25 decliners among index names), a healthier setup than a narrow momentum spike. Oil's reversal is the key swing factor to watch: Brent's jump back to $83 and WTI to $78 on Iran's conditional stance on a Hormuz reopening could revive Pakistan's import-bill and inflation concerns if it persists, working against the disinflation narrative that underpinned the SBP's recent rate hold. Sector leadership in banks, E&P, cement and fertiliser still points to broad-based rotation rather than narrow speculation. Watch 180,015 as the first floor; a close below re-opens 178,500. On the upside, clearing the psychological 182,000 mark keeps the index on track toward the year's 189,167 high set in January. All levels are indicative desk estimates, not recommendations.

🌅 Economic Vibes — Morning Brief | Friday, 07 August 2026

The KSE-100 stretched its rally to a fourth straight session while Wall Street cooled off from record highs and oil snapped back on renewed Hormuz uncertainty — here's what the desk is watching this morning.

THE OVERNIGHT TAPE
Dow -0.85% to 53,885 (pulling back after five record closes this week), S&P 500 -0.18% to 7,709.96, and Nasdaq -0.06% to 26,348.35, as rising Treasury yields (10Y 4.61%, 2Y ~4.18%) and a jump in oil prices weighed on sentiment even as softer ADP jobs data kept September rate-cut hopes alive.

PAKISTAN
KSE-100 gained 0.98% (+1,761.66 pts) to close at 181,776.59, a fourth straight advance on breadth-confirmed buying — 75 advancers vs 25 decliners among index names — led by banks, oil & gas E&P, cement, fertiliser and power on turnover of 345.78m shares (Rs40.31bn). CPI eased to 9.2% YoY in July from 11.1% in June, and the SBP held its policy rate at 11.5% for a second straight meeting; six-month KIBOR tracks near 11.70–11.90% (desk est.). USD/PKR ticked up modestly to 278.15 interbank.

GCC
OPEC+ agreed on 2 August to add a further 188,000 bpd from September. Saudi's non-oil PMI held near 53.1 in July while the UAE's climbed to a four-month high of 52.7. Saudi's PIF board approved its 2026-2030 strategy, pivoting from rapid project launches toward localisation, Saudisation and long-term industrial capability. Oil reversed higher — Brent +4.9% to $83.34, WTI +3.37% to $77.75 — after Iran tied any Hormuz reopening to the US lifting its naval blockade.

GLOBAL
Gold climbed to a seven-week high near $4,271 (+2.38%), and silver added 0.6% to $61.83, as haven demand stayed bid despite this week's record US equities. Washington's trade agenda keeps moving: a 50% Section 338 tariff on ~$20bn of Canadian dairy, alcohol and motor-vehicle exports lands in 12 days (19 August), while Pakistan's own reciprocal tariff with the US sits at a comparatively favourable 19%.

LEGISLATIVE TRACKER
Pakistan's Finance Act 2026 digital-creator withholding tax (5%/10%) continues to be deducted at source by banks, with a new IMF-linked tax-audit manual due by end-August.
Saudi's PIF 2026-2030 strategy shifts capital toward localisation even as Section 301 forced-labor duties keep Gulf exporters exposed.
The Canada tariff step-up (19 August) and Pakistan's 19% US tariff rate reshape relative trade competitiveness across textiles, dairy and autos.

THE DAY AHEAD
KSE-100: support 180,015 (Wednesday's close, deeper at 178,500), pivot 181,777 (Thursday's close), resistance 182,000 (psychological, then the 2026 high of 189,167 set in January).
Desk view: breadth-confirmed buying argues for a healthier tape, but oil's reversal on Hormuz conditions is the key swing factor for Pakistan's import bill and the disinflation narrative. All levels are indicative desk estimates, not recommendations.
